Q: Adobe Acrobat: Is there a way to get rid of the arrow of a dropdown after selecting an option that does not lock selecting a different option? A:

I've been struggling with this for a while and finally figured out a workaround (Joel's suggestion didn't work in my use case due to me needing this carrot to go away on print instead of on export and it seemed too late in the process for the javascript event to trigger).

What I did:

  1. Create my drop down field

    1. Set the form field option as "Visible but doesn't print".

    2. In the Text Field Properties > Validate tab, select Run custom validation script

      1. var f = this.getField("destinationFieldName");

switch (event.value) {
  case "option 1":
    f.value = "option 1";
    break;

  case "option 2":
    f.value = "option 2";
    break;

  default:
    f.value = "";
}

    3. In the Text Field Properties > Options tab, ensure Commit selected value immediately is checked

  2. Create a regular fillable field and put it directly on top of the drop down

    1. Set the form field option as "Hidden but printable"

Q: Does Unicode have a defined maximum number of code points? A:

The maximum valid code point in Unicode is U+10FFFF, which makes it a 21-bit code set (but not all 21-bit integers are valid Unicode code points; specifically the values from 0x110000 to 0x1FFFFF are not valid Unicode code points).

This is where the number 1,114,112 comes from: U+0000 .. U+10FFFF is 1,114,112 values.

However, there are also a set of code points that are the surrogates for UTF-16. These are in the range U+D800 .. U+DFFF. These are 2048 code points that are reserved for UTF-16.

1,114,112 - 2,048 = 1,112,064

There are also 66 non-characters. These are defined in part in Corrigendum #9: 34 values of the form U+nFFFE and U+nFFFF (where n is a value 0x00000, 0x10000, … 0xF0000, 0x100000), and 32 values U+FDD0 - U+FDEF. Subtracting those too yields 1,111,998 allocatable characters. There are three ranges reserved for 'private use': U+E000 .. U+F8FF, U+F0000 .. U+FFFFD, and U+100000 .. U+10FFFD. And the number of values actually assigned depends on the version of Unicode you're looking at. You can find information about the latest version at the Unicode Consortium. Amongst other things, the Introduction there says:

The Unicode Standard, Version 7.0, contains 112,956 characters

So only about 10% of the available code points have been allocated.

I can't account for why you found 1,112,114 as the number of code points.

Incidentally, the upper limit U+10FFFF is chosen so that all the values in Unicode can be represented in one or two 2-byte coding units in UTF-16, using one high surrogate and one low surrogate to represent values outside the BMP or Basic Multilingual Plane, which is the range U+0000 .. U+FFFF.

Q: How to split the words in oracle using regexp_substr? A:

This method allows you to iterate through the elements in the string, assuming the delimiter is a lower-case letter. Since there really is a null first element, start at the second element (level + 1). level is a built-in variable that comes along with the CONNECT BY syntax that starts at 1. The WITH just sets up test data. The REGEXP_SUBSTR( ) call returns the first group of the level+1 iteration of a string that is followed by a lowercase letter or the end of the string. REGEXP_COUNT( ) returns the number of delimiters.

with tbl(str) as (
  select 'aUNITED STATES :bUSCOMPANY,c7/1990.' from dual
)
select level as part_nbr, regexp_substr(str, '(.*?)([a-z]|$)', 1, level+1, null, 1) as part_name
from tbl
connect by level < REGEXP_COUNT(str ,'([a-z]|$)');


  PART_NBR PART_NAME                          
---------- -----------------------------------
         1 UNITED STATES :                    
         2 USCOMPANY,                         
         3 7/1990.                            

3 rows selected.

Q: Create a runtime location for a dynamic library using the nim FFI A:

I am unfamiliar with MacOS but I believe you are looking for the Windows equivalent of LoadLibraryA and a series of GetProcAddress .

Alternatively, I would assume that MacOS has a default lib search order that Nim inherits, you could either ensure the lib is in that search order somewhere, or when installing the app add the location of the lib to the search order.

Q: How to avoid Permission denied (publickey) SSH key (Windows) A:

Since this is the top answer on google, I'll just add a few details. I'm connecting from a Windows 11 (ssh client) to Windows Server 2019 (ssh server) with a separate non-admin user, enabled only keyauth and I always got "Permission denied (publickey)" when StrictModes = yes (default), but it worked when StrictModes = no. This might be a good check on your side, if you have the same problem, because if it works with "no", it means that your keys match (otherwise they don't). And if you are here at this point that the keys match, works without StrictModes and doesnt with "yes", it usually means there is a problem with file access permissions, like it was mentioned before.

Now, two kickers:

  1. OpenSSH StrictModes=yes allows only SYSTEM, Administrators group and the user connecting through SSH to file "authorized_keys" and it's parent folder (.ssh usually), maybe sometimes even a parent of the parent, but don't quote me on that.

  2. Now this one got me good. Owner of the file "authorized_keys" must be the same user that is trying to connect!!! Right click on the file > Properties > Security > Advanced and check on the top who the Owner is. When I fixed this, it started to work on StrictModes = yes. I made this file as an admin user and so the owner was not correctly set.
